questions.question: Match the following marked structures to the correct layers of the epidermis.
questions.explanation: The image is a histological section of epidermis. The marked layers correspond to stratum corneum, stratum granulosum, stratum spinosum, and stratum basale; therefore option D gives the correct mapping. Thin hairy skin has these four layers. Thick glabrous skin of palms and soles additionally has a clear stratum lucidum between stratum corneum and stratum granulosum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: Which of the following layers of epidermis is referred to as the prickle cell layer?
questions.explanation: Stratum spinosum is the prickle-cell layer. Its keratinocytes are attached by desmosomes. During H&E preparation the cells shrink away from one another except at these attachments, making the desmosomes appear as spines or prickles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: In which of the following layers of the epidermis are multiple layers of intertwining anucleate keratinocytes seen?
questions.explanation: Stratum corneum is composed of multiple layers of flattened, anucleate, keratinized cells that can intertwine. Keratinocytes originate in the stratum basale and progressively lose their nuclei and dehydrate as they migrate superficially. The thick stratum corneum contributes to the epidermal barrier against microbes and fluid loss.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: Given below is a histological section showing the layers of the skin. The region marked X points to the location of ______.
questions.explanation: The marked region points to intercellular adhesions formed by desmosomes. Desmosomes (maculae adherentes) are adhesive junctions that maintain mechanical integrity and resist shearing. They include desmosomal cadherins, cytoplasmic plaque proteins such as plakoglobin/plakophilin/desmoplakin, and keratin intermediate filaments. Hemidesmosomes instead mediate cell-to-extracellular-matrix adhesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: A young patient presented with an itchy, rough rash with silvery scales along the extensor surface of her elbows, knees and scalp. Histopathological examination of the skin sample showed marked elongation and clubbing of the structure marked X in the given image. Identify the structure marked X.
questions.explanation: The clinical picture is psoriasis. The marked structures are epidermal pegs (rete ridges), downward projections of epidermis between dermal papillae. Psoriasis characteristically shows elongation and clubbing of rete ridges.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: In which of the following layers of the skin are melanocytes present?
questions.explanation: Melanocytes are located in the stratum basale. They are neural-crest-derived cells that migrate to the basal epidermis during development. They synthesize melanin in melanosomes and transfer it through dendritic processes to surrounding keratinocytes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: Which of the following cells act as slow-adapting touch receptors?
questions.explanation: Merkel cells are slow-adapting mechanoreceptors involved in light touch. They are found in the stratum basale of highly sensitive skin, including fingertips and around hair follicles, and are contacted by unmyelinated sensory nerve endings.

questions.question: Identify the structure marked X in the given histological image of the dermis.
questions.explanation: The marked structure is a Pacinian corpuscle. It is a large onion-like receptor in the dermis and hypodermis, made of concentric lamellae of flattened Schwann cells and collagen around an axon. It is a rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor for coarse touch, pressure and vibration.

questions.question: Given below is an image of a histological section of the skin. Identify the structure marked X.
questions.explanation: The marked structure is a Meissner corpuscle in the papillary dermis. It has a connective-tissue capsule and a stack of modified Schwann cells. These rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors are specialized for light touch and low-frequency stimuli and are abundant in sensitive glabrous skin.

questions.question: Panniculus adiposus is present in:
questions.explanation: Panniculus adiposus is present in the axilla. It is a sheet of subcutaneous fat over most of the body and contributes to smooth skin contour. The source notes that it is absent in the scrotum, penis and eyelids.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man presented to the dermatology OPD with complaints of patchy hair loss. A punch biopsy of the scalp was taken to assess the cause of the hair loss. Given below is the histological section of the hair follicle. Identify the structure marked Y in the image.
questions.explanation: The marked structure is the outer root sheath. From the hair shaft outward, the source describes medulla, cortex, inner root sheath, outer root sheath, glassy membrane and connective-tissue sheath. Cells of the outer root sheath appear clear because they contain glycogen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes the arrector pili muscle?

options.text: Mixture of skeletal and smooth muscle, with dominant skeletal muscle
Mixture of skeletal and smooth muscle, with dominant smooth muscle

questions.explanation: Arrector pili are smooth muscles. They connect the undersurface of hair follicles to papillary dermis and are sympathetically innervated. Their contraction produces hair erection and goose flesh and helps squeeze sebaceous secretion into the follicle. The source notes their absence in several specialized hair regions.

questions.question: Identify the type of gland depicted in the schematic image.
questions.explanation: The schematic depicts an apocrine gland, in which the apical part of the secretory cell is shed during discharge. The source contrasts this with holocrine secretion, where the whole cell disintegrates, and merocrine secretion, where products are released by exocytosis while the cell remains intact.

questions.question: Given below is the histological section of the cornea. Identify the structures marked X and Y in the image.
questions.explanation: X and Y are the corneal endothelium and Bowman's membrane, respectively. From anterior to posterior the source lists corneal epithelium, Bowman's layer, corneal stroma (substantia propria), Descemet's membrane and corneal endothelium. It also notes the recently described pre-Descemet/Dua layer between stroma and Descemet's membrane.

questions.question: Arrange from outer to inner the layers of the retina given below: A-Retinal pigment epithelium; B-Inner plexiform layer; C-Nerve fiber layer; D-Inner nuclear layer; E-External limiting membrane.
questions.explanation: From outer to inner, the listed retinal layers are retinal pigment epithelium (A), external limiting membrane (E), inner nuclear layer (D), inner plexiform layer (B), and nerve fiber layer (C). Hence A-E-D-B-C is correct.

questions.question: Identify the structure shown in the histological image below.
questions.explanation: The histological image is the cochlea, identified by the organ of Corti. The cochlea makes about 2.75 turns around the modiolus. The vestibular and basilar membranes divide the bony labyrinth into scala vestibuli (perilymph), scala media (endolymph) and scala tympani (perilymph).

questions.chapter: Skin & Special Senses, Eye and Ear
questions.question: The gelatinous component of the crista ampullaris that extends from the crista to the roof of the ampulla is known as:
questions.explanation: The gelatinous component over the crista ampullaris is the cupula. Hair-cell stereocilia and kinocilium project into the cupula. During head rotation, lag of endolymph deflects the cupula and stimulates the hair cells, contributing to spatial orientation.
